John Mark
JON MARK
noun (figure)
John, Hebrew Yochanan, "the Lord is gracious"; Mark, Latin Marcus, his Roman surname. The two names mark his Jewish and Roman identity.

📖 Biblical Definition

John, whose surname was Mark, was the son of Mary of Jerusalem, in whose house the church gathered to pray when Peter was delivered from prison (Acts 12:12). He was kinsman to Barnabas and went with Paul and Barnabas as their minister on the first journey, but at Pamphylia "John departing from them returned to Jerusalem" (Acts 13:13). When Barnabas would take him again, the contention was so sharp that Paul and Barnabas parted, "and so Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus" (Acts 15:39). Yet this was not the end of the man. Grace restored him: Paul later names Mark among his fellow-labourers, and at the last writes, "Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry" (2 Tim 4:11). Peter calls him "Marcus my son" (1 Pet 5:13), and the church has ever received him as the writer of the second Gospel. Thus John Mark is a standing testimony of restoration after failure. This dictionary confesses that the Lord does not cast off His servants for a single faltering, but in His grace recovers and reuses those who once turned back, making the unprofitable profitable for the ministry.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The son of Mary of Jerusalem and kinsman of Barnabas, whose desertion at Pamphylia occasioned the Paul-Barnabas contention; later restored as profitable for the ministry, and the writer of the Gospel of Mark.

expand to see more

JOHN MARK, noun. The son of Mary of Jerusalem, kinsman of Barnabas, and writer of the second Gospel.

First seen in Acts 12:12, where the church prayed in his mother's house for Peter's release.

He departed from Paul and Barnabas at Pamphylia, occasioning their sharp contention.

Restored by grace, he became one of whom Paul wrote, "he is profitable to me for the ministry."

Peter called him "Marcus my son," and through him the Gospel of Mark was given to the church.

📖 Key Scripture

Acts 12:12 — "And when he had considered the thing, he came to the house of Mary the mother of John, whose surname was Mark; where many were gathered together praying."

Acts 13:13 — "Now when Paul and his company loosed from Paphos, they came to Perga in Pamphylia: and John departing from them returned to Jerusalem."

Acts 15:39 — "And the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other: and so Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus."

2 Tim 4:11 — "Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the lesson is the recovery of biblical restoration after failure, neither excusing the fault nor despairing of the man.

expand to see more

John Mark is not the subject of modern ideological dispute, but his story is often mishandled in two directions. Some excuse his desertion as nothing, dissolving the seriousness that made Paul refuse to take him again; others harden it into a permanent verdict, as if a man who once turned back could never be useful. Scripture allows neither. The departure was a real fault, grievous enough to part two great men; yet it was not final, for grace restored him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the doctrine of restoration. The God who perseveres with His own does not discard them for a single failure; He chastens, recovers, and reuses. Mark, once the cause of contention and called by implication unprofitable, ends as "profitable to me for the ministry" and the penman of a Gospel. This rebukes both the leniency that winks at desertion and the rigor that writes men off, and it comforts every faltering servant with the certainty that the Lord finishes the work He begins.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

John renders Hebrew Yochanan, the Lord is gracious; Mark is the Latin Marcus.

expand to see more

John is the Hebrew Yochanan, "the Lord is gracious," his Jewish name.

Mark is the Latin Marcus, his Roman surname, fitting a dweller in the Empire.

Acts 13:5 calls him their hupēretēs, minister or attendant, on the first journey.

Acts 13:13 uses apochōrēsas, having departed, of his turning back at Pamphylia.

His double name roots him in both the covenant people and the wider Gentile world he served.

Usage

"John Mark turned back at Pamphylia, but grace later restored him to fruitful ministry."

"The contention over John Mark parted Paul and Barnabas at the start of the second journey."

"Peter's affection for John Mark, "Marcus my son," shaped the Gospel that bears his name."
